idiom_name: sealed trait per grammar category + case class per rule + recursive match
implementation_notes: Scala's algebraic data types plus pattern matching are the local idiom: a sealed trait per grammar category, case classes per rule, and a recursive match as the evaluator. The compiler reports non-exhaustive matches and with -Xfatal-warnings (or Scala 3's stricter analysis) a new case class fails the build instead of raising MatchError at run time. Keeping evaluation outside the nodes lets several interpreters share one tree - the documented reason Scala ports replace the classic visitor with pattern matching.
code_sketch:
sealed trait Expr
case class Num(value: Int) extends Expr
case class Add(left: Expr, right: Expr) extends Expr
case class Var(name: String) extends Expr
def eval(e: Expr, ctx: Map[String, Int]): Int = e match {
  case Num(v)      => v
  case Add(l, r)   => eval(l, ctx) + eval(r, ctx)
  case Var(name)   => ctx.getOrElse(name, throw new NoSuchElementException(name))
}
pitfalls: A non-exhaustive match is a warning by default; without -Xfatal-warnings a new case class slips through as a MatchError on the first evaluation.
Case classes are structural, so patterns bind to constructor arity and order: adding a field to a node breaks every extractor that destructured it.
Recursion is not trampolined: deep expressions overflow the stack, and Scala's stack is fixed; use an explicit work list for untrusted input.

variants.name: Scala 3 enum with parameterised cases
variants.idiom_name: enum Expr with parameterised cases + match
variants.implementation_notes: Scala 3 folds the ADT into one declaration: an enum whose cases carry parameters replaces the sealed trait plus case objects, and exhaustiveness reporting for match is the same. It is the shorter, clearer form on a Scala 3 codebase; on cross-built libraries the sealed trait form is the portable one, and Java interop of enums is weaker than that of sealed traits.
variants.code_sketch:
enum Expr:
  case Num(value: Int)
  case Add(left: Expr, right: Expr)
  case Mul(left: Expr, right: Expr)
def eval(e: Expr): Int = e match
  case Expr.Num(v)    => v
  case Expr.Add(l, r) => eval(l) + eval(r)
  case Expr.Mul(l, r) => eval(l) * eval(r)
pitfalls: Enum cases are not case classes: copy and product extractors do not behave identically, so code ported from a sealed trait hierarchy needs revisiting.
Enums live in the same source file unless cases are declared in the companion (Scala 3.2+); plan the file layout before the grammar grows.
Java interop is weaker than for sealed traits, which matters when the AST crosses an API boundary consumed by Java code.
